item.content:encoded:
IRR urges Minister Thembi Simelane to prioritise women’s property rightsAug 12, 2026

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-12

The Institute of Race Relations (IRR) will be writing to Minister of Human Settlements Thembi Simelane this week to urge her to speed up the process of extending property rights, especially to women.

Says IRR Strategic Engagements Manager Makone Maja: “Celebrating Women’s Month without guaranteeing rights that are integral to women’s safety, dignity and financial security is meaningless, especially in a country such as ours where 46% of households are women-led. When women are not safe, neither are their children or their families.”

As of May 2026, the housing backlog in South Africa was a towering 2.6 million, according to the Minister. This is a crisis that confronts over 12 million people who live in fear, uncertainty, and unstable and unsafe living conditions.

Maja says: “The Minister still relies on the excuse of apartheid spatial inequality for the slow roll out of housing development, yet she is a member of a party that was kept in power for 30 uninterrupted years of majority government on the strength of promising to eradicate the issues apartheid caused.

“South Africans must see the apartheid blame game for what it truly is – the government’s excuse for its own bureaucratic deficiencies that cause implementation delays and ultimately lead to its failure to deliver.”

item.title: [South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa] The Hoernlé Memorial Lectures
item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
The Hoernlé Memorial Lectures

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-12

The inaugural Hoernlé lecture was delivered by Jan Hendrik Hofmeyr, IRR vice-president and honorary life member, in 1945 on the topic of “Christian principles and race problems”. Other distinguished speakers included IRR co-founder Professor Edgar Brookes on the Institute’s first 21 years in “We come of age” (1950), Archbishop Dennis Hurley on “Apartheid: A crisis of the Christian conscience” (1964), Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi on “White and black nationalism, ethnicity and the future of the homelands” (1974), Dr Alan Paton on “Towards racial justice: Will there be a change of heart?” (1979) and again on “Federation or desolation” (1985) – the only speaker to have delivered two Hoernlé lectures – Professor Jonathan Jansen on “When does a university cease to exist?” (2005) and Professor RW Johnson on “The future of the liberal tradition in South Africa” (2011).

The speakers often tackled thorny questions relating to race, ideology and South Africa’s future. In their explorations, they reflected the most pressing preoccupations of their times, giving us a window into the past that shows contemporary views on issues that often seemed intractable at the time. It is sobering to look back from today’s vantage point and realise how far South Africa has come – and how much still remains to be done to create a free and prosperous South Africa for all.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
History of the IRR Bursary Programme (1936-2022)

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-12

From a time of simple racial segregation in the first part of the twentieth century, through the intensified racial regime of the apartheid period and for nearly three decades into post-apartheid democracy, about 6,000 black South Africans graduated from universities, technikons and other tertiary institutions thanks to the bursary programme administered by the South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR). Immense hurdles had to be overcome, both by the students themselves as well as funders and administrators.

While unquestionably delivering positive outcomes, the programme was often caught up in the turbulence of the times, especially during the popular resistance from the mid-1970s to the early 1990s. If not itself the subject of controversy, it was often linked to controversy and conflict around matters like reform versus revolution, disinvestment versus business influence, and armed struggle versus peaceful resistance. This is the story of that bursary programme and the tumultuous times in which it operated.

The South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR) is a classically liberal not-for-profit organisation, founded in 1929 with the objective of improving relations between South Africa's race groups. This almost immediately became a matter of opposing racial discrimination and promoting the establishment of a non-racial society in South Africa.
